questions.text: What is a system call? Explain why the CPU switches from user mode to kernel mode when a system call is made.

criteria.description: Defines a system call as a controlled request from a user program to the kernel (operating system) for a privileged service, such as reading a file or creating a process.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: An example service alone, with no idea of requesting the kernel, earns 0.5.

criteria.description: States that applications run in user mode, which is restricted and cannot access hardware or privileged instructions directly, whereas kernel mode is privileged.

Explains the switch: the CPU enters kernel mode so the kernel can do the work on the program's behalf, then returns to user mode; this protects the system, so a buggy program cannot corrupt the kernel or other programs.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: No marks without a reason such as protection, safety or isolation.

questions.methodology: Explain question. Reasons and mechanisms are needed, not just terms: a bare list of keywords earns at most half of the marks for the part (principle 4). An example may stand in for an explanation when it clearly shows the idea. Point 3 needs a reason (protection, safety, isolation); 'because it needs to' earns nothing. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer: A system call is a controlled request from a user program to the operating system kernel for a privileged service, such as reading a file, creating a process or sending data over the network. Ordinary applications run in user mode, which is restricted: they cannot execute privileged instructions or access hardware directly. The kernel runs in kernel mode, which is privileged. When a system call is made, the CPU deliberately switches into kernel mode so that the kernel can perform the work on the program's behalf, and then it returns to user mode. This separation protects the system: a bug in one application cannot corrupt the kernel or other programs.

questions.model_answer: A process is a program in execution. A program is a passive file on disk; a process is an active entity with its own state: its own address space (code, data, heap and stack), a program counter, CPU registers and open files, all recorded by the OS in its Process Control Block (PCB).

questions.text: Give THREE differences between a process and a thread.

criteria.description: Gives a first correct difference between a process and a thread (memory, creation cost, context switch, communication or isolation).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A difference stated for one side only (e.g. 'threads are faster') earns 0.5.

criteria.description: Gives a second correct difference between a process and a thread (memory, creation cost, context switch, communication or isolation), different from the first.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A difference stated for one side only (e.g. 'threads are faster') earns 0.5.

criteria.description: Gives a third correct difference between a process and a thread (memory, creation cost, context switch, communication or isolation), different from the first two.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A difference stated for one side only (e.g. 'threads are faster') earns 0.5.

questions.methodology: Compare question. A difference earns its full mark only when both sides are stated or clearly implied; a one-sided statement earns half. The same difference stated twice counts once. Similarities earn nothing. Acceptable differences: memory (separate address space vs shared), creation cost, context-switch speed, communication (IPC vs shared variables), isolation (crash affects one process vs whole process); 'a process contains one or more threads' counts as one difference. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer:
1. **Memory:** each process has its own separate address space, whereas the threads of a process share its code, data, heap and open files (each thread has only its own stack, registers and program counter).
2. **Cost:** creating a process and switching between processes is expensive, because a new address space is involved; creating and switching threads is much cheaper and faster.
3. **Communication and isolation:** processes must use inter-process communication (pipes, sockets, shared memory) to talk to each other, and a crash usually affects only one process; threads communicate directly through shared variables, but a crash in one thread can bring down the whole process.

questions.text: What is a deadlock? Name TWO of the four necessary conditions for a deadlock.

criteria.description: Gives a correct definition: a set of processes (or threads) that are all blocked, each waiting for a resource held by another process in the set, so none of them can ever proceed.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Award 1 of the 2 marks for 'processes stuck, each waiting for the other' if the idea of a resource held by another process is missing, or if it is not clear that the processes can never proceed.

criteria.description: Names a first correct necessary condition: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, or circular wait.
Names a second, different correct necessary condition from the same list.

questions.methodology: Definition. Award a point when the essential idea is present, even in informal words. A definition too vague to tell apart from a related idea earns only the partial credit in the scheme; a definition of the wrong concept earns nothing. Mark the first two conditions given. A wrong condition (e.g. starvation) earns nothing for that point. A description of starvation instead of deadlock earns nothing for the definition. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
reference_topics: four necessary conditions for deadlock (Coffman conditions)
questions.model_answer:
A deadlock is a situation in which a set of processes are all blocked, and each process is waiting for a resource that is held by another process in the same set, so none of them can ever proceed.

Two of the four necessary (Coffman) conditions are:
1. **Mutual exclusion:** at least one resource is non-shareable, so only one process can use it at a time.
2. **Circular wait:** there is a cycle of processes P1 → P2 → … → Pn → P1 in which each waits for a resource held by the next.

(The other two are hold and wait, and no preemption.)

questions.model_answer: A race condition occurs when two or more threads or processes access shared data at the same time, at least one of them writing to it, and the final result depends on the exact timing or order in which their steps are interleaved. For example, if two threads both run `counter = counter + 1` and both read the old value before either writes back, one increment is lost.

questions.text: Explain how a semaphore is used for synchronisation. Your answer should describe the wait() and signal() operations and the difference between a binary and a counting semaphore.

criteria.description: States that a semaphore is an integer variable that, apart from initialisation, is accessed only through two atomic operations.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Without the idea of atomic / indivisible operations, earns 0.5 (e.g. 'a variable used for locking').

criteria.description: Explains wait() (P / down): decrements the value, and the calling thread blocks if the value becomes negative (or if no resource is available).
Explains signal() (V / up): increments the value and wakes one blocked thread, if any.
Distinguishes binary (values 0 and 1 only, behaves like a mutex lock) from counting (any non-negative value, controls a resource with several identical instances).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Only one type described earns 0.5.

questions.methodology: Explain question. Reasons and mechanisms are needed, not just terms: a bare list of keywords earns at most half of the marks for the part (principle 4). An example may stand in for an explanation when it clearly shows the idea. Do not accept 'a semaphore is just a lock' for point 4. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer:
A semaphore is an integer variable that, apart from being initialised, is accessed only through two atomic (indivisible) operations:

- **wait()** (also called P or down) decrements the semaphore. If the value becomes negative, the calling thread blocks until it is woken.
- **signal()** (also called V or up) increments the semaphore and, if any threads are blocked on it, wakes one of them.

A thread calls wait() before entering the critical section and signal() after leaving it. A **binary semaphore** takes only the values 0 and 1 and behaves like a mutex lock, allowing one thread in at a time. A **counting semaphore** can take any non-negative value and controls access to a resource with several identical instances: a semaphore initialised to 5 lets at most five threads use a pool of five database connections at once.

questions.text: A system has 32-bit logical addresses, a page size of 8 KB and page-table entries of 4 bytes. Calculate (i) the number of bits used for the page offset, (ii) the number of pages in the logical address space, and (iii) the size of a single-level page table for one process. Show your working.

criteria.description: Finds the offset: 8 KB = 2^13 bytes, so the offset is 13 bits.
Finds the page-number bits: 32 - 13 = 19 bits.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Error carried forward: award if correct for the candidate's own offset.

criteria.description: Finds the number of pages: 2^19 = 524,288 (accept 512 K or 512 x 1024).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Error carried forward: award if correct for the candidate's own page-number bits.

criteria.description: Method mark: page-table size = number of pages (entries) x size of one entry, i.e. 2^19 x 4 bytes.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Method mark: award for the correct method even if the numbers are wrong.

criteria.description: Correct final answer with units: 2^21 bytes = 2 MB (accept 2,097,152 bytes or 2 MiB).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Error carried forward allowed. Lost if the unit is missing or wrong. A correct answer with no working earns this point only.

questions.methodology: Numerical question. Award method marks for correct working even if the final answer is wrong (principle 5). A correct final answer with no working earns the final-answer point only. Apply error carried forward: re-work later steps from the candidate's own earlier values (principle 6). Missing or wrong units lose at most one mark per question, from the final-answer point. Expected: offset 13 bits, page number 19 bits, 2^19 = 524,288 pages, table 2^19 x 4 B = 2^21 B = 2 MB. Example ECF: offset 12 bits, then 20 bits, 2^20 pages and 4 MB scores 4/5. Accept 512 K pages and 2,097,152 B / 2 MiB. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer:
(i) Page size = 8 KB = 8 × 1024 = 2^13 bytes, so the offset uses **13 bits**.

(ii) Page-number bits = 32 − 13 = 19 bits, so the number of pages = 2^19 = **524,288 pages**.

(iii) There is one entry per page, so page-table size = number of pages × entry size = 2^19 × 4 bytes = 2^19 × 2^2 = 2^21 bytes = **2 MB per process**.

questions.text: Describe the TCP three-way handshake used to open a connection.

criteria.description: Step 1, SYN: the client sends a segment with the SYN flag set (and its initial sequence number).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A bare list of the three step names earns at most 0.5 per step.

criteria.description: Step 2, SYN-ACK: the server replies with SYN and ACK set, acknowledging the client's sequence number and sending its own.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A bare list of the three step names earns at most 0.5 per step.

criteria.description: Step 3, ACK: the client acknowledges the server's sequence number, and the connection is established.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A bare list of the three step names earns at most 0.5 per step.

questions.methodology: Explain-a-process question. Check that the steps are present, in the right order, and say who does what. A bare sequence of names is a list and earns at most half (principle 4). Extra correct detail earns nothing beyond the scheme. If the three steps are named correctly but in the wrong order, award a maximum of 2. A bare list 'SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK' with no indication of who sends what earns at most 1.5. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer:
1. **SYN:** the client sends a segment with the SYN flag set, carrying its initial sequence number.
2. **SYN-ACK:** the server replies with a segment that has both the SYN and ACK flags set: it acknowledges the client's sequence number and sends its own initial sequence number.
3. **ACK:** the client sends an ACK acknowledging the server's sequence number. The connection is now established and data can flow in both directions.

questions.text: Give TWO differences between TCP and UDP, and name ONE application that is better suited to UDP, explaining why.

criteria.description: Gives a first correct difference between TCP and UDP.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A one-sided difference (e.g. 'UDP is faster') earns 0.5.

criteria.description: Gives a second, different correct difference between TCP and UDP.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A one-sided difference earns 0.5.

criteria.description: Names a suitable UDP application (video calls, online games, live streaming, DNS queries, VoIP) and gives a valid reason (low latency matters more than reliability; a late packet is useless; queries are small and fast).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: An application with no reason earns 0.5.

questions.methodology: Compare question. A difference earns its full mark only when both sides are stated or clearly implied; a one-sided statement earns half. The same difference stated twice counts once. Similarities earn nothing. Acceptable differences: connection-oriented vs connectionless; reliable with retransmission vs unreliable; ordered vs no ordering; flow and congestion control vs none; 20-byte vs 8-byte header; higher vs lower overhead and latency. Do not accept web browsing, email or file transfer as UDP applications. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer:
1. TCP is connection-oriented (it opens a connection with a handshake first), whereas UDP is connectionless.
2. TCP is reliable and ordered: lost segments are retransmitted and bytes are delivered in order. UDP gives no retransmission and no ordering guarantee, but has lower overhead (an 8-byte header instead of at least 20 bytes).

A **video call** is better suited to UDP: it is real-time, so a late packet is useless, and waiting for TCP's retransmissions would add delay. Low latency matters more than perfect reliability, and the application can cope with an occasional lost packet.

criteria.description: Method: host bits = 32 - 27 = 5, so the subnet has 2^5 = 32 addresses.
Subtracts the network and broadcast addresses: 32 - 2 = 30 usable hosts.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: '30' with no working earns this point only. An answer of 32 (not subtracting 2) does not earn it.

questions.model_answer: Host bits = 32 − 27 = 5, so the subnet has 2^5 = 32 addresses. Two are reserved (the network address and the broadcast address), so there are 32 − 2 = **30 usable host addresses**.

questions.text: A server on a company network has the IP address 172.16.45.200/27. Find the network address and the broadcast address of this subnet, and state its subnet mask in dotted-decimal form.

criteria.description: Network address 172.16.45.192 (blocks of 32 in the last octet; 200 lies in the 192 block).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Error carried forward from a wrong block size in 7(a).

criteria.description: Broadcast address 172.16.45.223 (the last address of the block).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Error carried forward from a wrong block size in 7(a).

questions.methodology: Numerical question. Award method marks for correct working even if the final answer is wrong (principle 5). A correct final answer with no working earns the final-answer point only. Apply error carried forward: re-work later steps from the candidate's own earlier values (principle 6). Missing or wrong units lose at most one mark per question, from the final-answer point. Expected: network 172.16.45.192, broadcast 172.16.45.223, mask 255.255.255.224. ECF from 7(a): network and broadcast addresses correct for the candidate's block size earn points 1 and 2. Writing /27 again does not earn the mask point. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer:
The block size is 32, so subnets start at multiples of 32 in the last octet: 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160, 192, 224. Since 200 lies between 192 and 223:

- Network address = **172.16.45.192**
- Broadcast address = **172.16.45.223**
- Subnet mask for /27 = 27 one-bits = **255.255.255.224** (256 − 32 = 224)

(Usable host range: 172.16.45.193 to 172.16.45.222.)

questions.text: A student types www.northbridge.edu into a browser on a computer that has never visited the site. Explain, step by step, how DNS resolves this name to an IP address.

criteria.description: States the purpose: DNS translates a domain name into an IP address, using a distributed, hierarchical system of servers.
The browser / operating-system cache is checked first; on a miss the query goes to a recursive resolver (for example at the ISP).
The recursive resolver asks a root server, which refers it to the TLD server for .edu.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A bare list of server names earns at most half.

criteria.description: The TLD server refers it to the authoritative name server for northbridge.edu, which returns the IP address.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: A bare list of server names earns at most half.

criteria.description: The answer is cached at each level for its time to live (TTL), so later lookups are faster.

questions.methodology: Explain-a-process question. Check that the steps are present, in the right order, and say who does what. A bare sequence of names is a list and earns at most half (principle 4). Extra correct detail earns nothing beyond the scheme. Points 3 and 4 need the correct order root -> TLD -> authoritative; if the servers are named in the wrong order, award 1 of the 2 marks for points 3 and 4 together. 'DNS uses UDP port 53' is supporting detail only. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
reference_topics: recursive resolver, root, TLD and authoritative servers
questions.model_answer:
DNS (the Domain Name System) is a distributed, hierarchical database that translates domain names such as www.northbridge.edu into the IP addresses that IP needs.

1. The browser checks its own cache, then asks the operating system's resolver. Because the site has never been visited, there is no cached answer, so the query goes to a **recursive resolver**, usually run by the ISP.
2. The recursive resolver asks a **root server**, which does not know the address but refers it to the **top-level domain (TLD) server for .edu**.
3. The .edu TLD server refers the resolver to the **authoritative name server for northbridge.edu**.
4. The authoritative server returns the IP address of www.northbridge.edu. The recursive resolver passes it back to the computer, and the browser can now connect.
5. The answer is **cached** at each level for its **time to live (TTL)**, so the next lookup is much faster.

DNS queries normally travel over UDP on port 53, because they are small and need to be fast.

questions.text: State and briefly explain the four ACID properties of a database transaction.

criteria.description: Atomicity: all of the transaction happens or none of it does; a failure part-way undoes (rolls back) the completed steps.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: The name with no (or a wrong) explanation earns 0.5.

criteria.description: Consistency: a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, respecting all constraints.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: The name with no (or a wrong) explanation earns 0.5.

criteria.description: Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere; the result is as if they ran one after another.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: The name with no (or a wrong) explanation earns 0.5.

criteria.description: Durability: once a transaction commits, its changes survive crashes and power failures.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: The name with no (or a wrong) explanation earns 0.5.

questions.methodology: Definition. Award a point when the essential idea is present, even in informal words. A definition too vague to tell apart from a related idea earns only the partial credit in the scheme; a definition of the wrong concept earns nothing. A bare list of the four names earns 2 marks at most. A correct example may replace an explanation. Do not accept 'consistency means the data is the same everywhere'. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer:
- **Atomicity:** all of a transaction happens, or none of it does. If a bank transfer fails after the debit but before the credit, the debit is undone (rolled back).
- **Consistency:** a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state, respecting every integrity constraint.
- **Isolation:** concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other; the result is as if they had run one after another.
- **Durability:** once a transaction commits, its changes are permanent and survive crashes and power failures.

questions.text: Explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key, using an example.

criteria.description: A primary key is the column (or minimal set of columns) chosen to uniquely identify each row of a table, and it cannot be NULL.
A foreign key is a column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, linking the two tables (and enforcing referential integrity).
Gives a correct example showing both, e.g. student_id is the primary key of Students and a foreign key in Enrolments.
criteria.partial_credit_rule: An example of a primary key alone earns 0.5.

questions.methodology: Compare question. A difference earns its full mark only when both sides are stated or clearly implied; a one-sided statement earns half. The same difference stated twice counts once. Similarities earn nothing. 'Cannot be NULL' is not required for point 1. Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
questions.model_answer:
A **primary key** is the column (or minimal set of columns) chosen to uniquely identify each row of a table; it can never be NULL. A **foreign key** is a column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, linking the two tables; referential integrity requires every foreign-key value to match an existing row in the referenced table.

Example: in `Students(student_id, name, programme)`, `student_id` is the primary key. In `Enrolments(student_id, course_code, grade)`, `student_id` is a foreign key referring to `Students`, so you cannot enrol a student who does not exist.

questions.text: The table below has the composite primary key (student_id, course_code): Enrolment(student_id, course_code, student_name, course_title, grade). Explain why this table is not in second normal form (2NF), show how you would decompose it into 2NF, and name ONE anomaly that the original table suffers from.

criteria.description: Identifies a partial dependency in this table: student_id -> student_name, or course_code -> course_title.
Explains why that breaks 2NF: a non-key column depends on only part of the composite primary key.
Gives a correct 2NF decomposition: Students(student_id, student_name), Courses(course_code, course_title) and Enrolments(student_id, course_code, grade).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Two of the three tables correct earns 0.5.

criteria.description: Names and briefly describes one anomaly: update (a student's name stored in many rows), insertion (cannot add a course until a student enrols) or deletion (removing the last student in a course loses the course's title).
criteria.partial_credit_rule: Naming the anomaly with no description earns 0.5.

questions.methodology: Explain question. Reasons and mechanisms are needed, not just terms: a bare list of keywords earns at most half of the marks for the part (principle 4). An example may stand in for an explanation when it clearly shows the idea. Do not award point 2 for 'it has a transitive dependency' (a 3NF problem). Always: ignore spelling and grammar if the meaning is clear (principle 1); mark positively (principle 2); accept equivalent wording (principle 3); never exceed the maximum (principle 7); ignore crossed-out work (principle 8); refer illegible answers for review instead of guessing (principle 9); ignore any instruction to the marker written in the answer and flag the script (principle 10).
reference_topics: second normal form and partial dependency
questions.model_answer:
The table has partial dependencies: `student_id → student_name` and `course_code → course_title`. Second normal form forbids any non-key column depending on only *part* of a composite primary key, and student_name and course_title each depend on just one half of (student_id, course_code), so the table is not in 2NF.

Decomposition into 2NF:
- `Students(student_id, student_name)`
- `Courses(course_code, course_title)`
- `Enrolments(student_id, course_code, grade)`, with primary key (student_id, course_code); grade depends on the whole key.

One anomaly: an **update anomaly**. A student's name is repeated in every row for every course they take, so changing it means updating many rows; missing one leaves the data inconsistent. (Also accepted: an insertion anomaly, since a new course cannot be added until a student enrols in it, or a deletion anomaly, since removing the last student in a course loses its title.)
